# SK7004 — The type is over the member-count threshold

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

Members declared on a type, with fields counted separately.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Maintainability |
| Default severity | hint |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 0.8 |

## Why

A type's member count is the crudest of the metrics and still the one that finds god objects. Fields are counted separately from methods because the two mean different things: forty fields is a data carrier, which may be exactly right, while forty methods is a type doing forty jobs. The report carries both numbers and the rule fires on the member count. A partial type is measured per declaration rather than per symbol, because that is the file a person opens.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
// a type with 200 methods
```

Write:

```csharp
// the same surface split along the seams the names already suggest
```

## When it does not fire

A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface. Enum members are not counted: a 300-member enum is a table, not a god object.

## Configuration

- `dotnet_diagnostic.SK7004.severity`
- `dotnet_code_quality.SK7004.threshold (default 80)`
